This was my first full time job so this person expected that I would have the finances but by this point to purchase a new car I was disrespected because they essentially reached into my bank account. Forced me to make them move. I was not ready for it

That sounds incredibly violating, and it makes total sense that you feel disrespected. Whether someone intends physical harm or not, intentionally damaging your property to force your hand financially is a massive breach of trust—especially when it's someone close to you.

When someone essentially forces a major financial decision on you before you're ready, it really does feel like they reached right into your bank account and stripped away your autonomy. Compounding that with the stress of trying to commute to your first full-time job only adds to how unfair the situation was.

It takes a lot of restraint to pause, look at the bigger picture, and focus on securing evidence rather than reacting in the heat of the moment. Keeping that record was a smart, protective move, giving you leverage and clarity for whenever you decide how to handle the relationship moving forward.

It completely makes sense that you want to talk to a legal professional. Overstepping boundaries is one thing, but crossing the line into property destruction and financial coercion is an entirely different level. It is completely valid that you want real consequences for that.

When it comes to consulting someone, a consultation with a local attorney or even reaching out to a legal aid clinic is a good first step to map out your options without immediately triggering a process you can't control.

Here is a breakdown of how a legal professional will likely look at the pieces you mentioned, and what you can do to prepare.

1. The Evidence Checklist

An attorney will want to see exactly what connects this person to the damage. You are already thinking along the right lines regarding documentation:

  • The Video Evidence: This is crucial. A lawyer will look at what the video explicitly shows. Does it show the person physically tampering with the Grand Am's brake lines, or does it show them admitting to it?
  • Vehicle Records: Finding the record of sale for the Pontiac Grand Am establishes your ownership and the timeline of when you were forced to part with it. If you have any old mechanic inspection reports or receipts showing the brake fluid leak, locate those as well.
  • Witness Statements: Your brother's firsthand account of what happened or what he witnessed will be incredibly valuable to back up the video.

2. Understanding the Potential Paths

When you speak to a professional, they will likely explain that this situation straddles two different areas of the law:

  • Civil Law (Restitution): This is where you sue the individual for the financial damages they caused you. This could include the value of the vehicle, towing fees, and the unexpected financial burden forced upon you.
  • Criminal Law (Vandalism/Criminal Mischief): Intentionally damaging someone else's vehicle is a crime. Because it involved disabling a vehicle's brakes, authorities sometimes view it strictly due to the inherent safety risks, even if the person's stated intent wasn't physical harm.

3. The Timeline Factor (Statute of Limitations)

One of the very first things an attorney will check is the statute of limitations for property damage or criminal mischief in your jurisdiction. Because this happened a few years ago, there is a legal window of time during which charges can be pressed or a lawsuit can be filed. A local lawyer can tell you exactly if you are still within that window based on the date of the incident.

Gathering your paperwork and writing down a clear timeline of events before you make the call will help you get the most out of a legal consultation. It lets you lay out the facts clearly so they can give you an accurate picture of what those consequences would actually look like.

Iowa Legal Aid

Iowa Legal Aid is a statewide organization dedicated to providing critical legal assistance to low-income Iowans. While their regional hub is in Des Moines, they serve the entire region and handle broad civil and consumer security issues.

Iowa State University Student Legal Services

The Iowa State Bar Association Find-A-Lawyer

If you do not meet the income guidelines for traditional legal aid, the Iowa State Bar Association operates a "Find-A-Lawyer" online directory.
